question.full_text:
The magnetic potential energy stored in a certain induction is $25\,\mathrm{Mj}$, when the current in the inductors is $60\,\mathrm{Ma}$. This inductors is of inductance
(1) $13.89\,\mathrm{H}$
(2) $0.138\,\mathrm{H}$
(3) $1.389\,\mathrm{H}$
(4) $138.88\,\mathrm{H}$
question.html:

  4. (4)138.88 H
question.stem: The magnetic potential energy stored in a certain induction is $25\,\mathrm{Mj}$, when the current in the inductors is $60\,\mathrm{Ma}$. This inductors is of inductance

solution.html:
1. U = 12LI2
  2. 25× 10-3 = 12L(60× 10-3)2
  3. ⇒ L = 50× 10-33600× 10-6
  4. = 25× 10103
  5. = 13.89 H
steps: $\Rightarrow L = \frac{50\times 10^{-3}}{3600\times 10^{-6}}$
Energy stored in an inductor: $U = \frac{1}{2} L I^2$.
Rearrange for inductance: $L = \frac{2U}{I^2}$.
Substitute $U = 25\,\mathrm{mJ} = 25 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{J}$ and $I = 60\,\mathrm{mA} = 60 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{A}$: $L = \frac{2 \times 25 \times 10^{-3}}{(60 \times 10^{-3})^2}$.
$L = \frac{0.05}{3.6 \times 10^{-3}} = 13.89\,\mathrm{H}$, which is option $1$.

  2. Rearrange for inductance: L = 2UI2.
  3. Substitute U = 25 mJ = 25 × 10-3 J and I = 60 mA = 60 × 10-3 A: L = 2 × 25 × 10-3(60 × 10-3)2.
  4. L = 0.053.6 × 10-3 = 13.89 H, which is option 1.

question.full_text:
An object is placed at a distance of $40\,\mathrm{cm}$ from a concave mirror of focal length $15\,\mathrm{cm}$ If the object is displaced through a distance of $20\,\mathrm{cm}$ towards the mirrors, the displacement of the image will be
(1) $36\,\mathrm{cm}$ towards the mirror
(2) $30\,\mathrm{cm}$ away from the mirror
(3) $30\,\mathrm{cm}$ towards the mirror
(4) $36\,\mathrm{cm}$ away from the mirror
question.html:
An object is placed at a distance of 40 cm from a concave mirror of focal length 15 cm If the object is displaced through a distance of 20 cm towards the mirrors, the displacement of the image will be
  1. (1)36 cm towards the mirror
  2. (2)30 cm away from the mirror
  3. (3)30 cm towards the mirror
  4. (4)36 cm away from the mirror
question.stem: An object is placed at a distance of $40\,\mathrm{cm}$ from a concave mirror of focal length $15\,\mathrm{cm}$ If the object is displaced through a distance of $20\,\mathrm{cm}$ towards the mirrors, the displacement of the image will be

solution.full_text:
1. $\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{q}$
2. $\Rightarrow -\frac{1}{15} = \frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{40}$
3. $\Rightarrow \frac{1}{v} = -\frac{1}{15} + \frac{1}{40}$
4. $\Rightarrow v = \frac{-600}{25}$
5. $v = -24\,\mathrm{cm}$
6. Finally $\frac{1}{15} = \frac{1}{v^{1}} - \frac{1}{20}$
7. $\Rightarrow -\frac{1}{15} + \frac{1}{20} = \frac{1}{v^{1}}$
8. $\Rightarrow v^{1} = \frac{300}{5}$
9. So image is displaced by $36\,\mathrm{cm}$ away from mirror (d)
solution.html:
1. 1f = 1v + 1q
  2. ⇒ -115 = 1v - 140
  3. ⇒ 1v = -115 + 140
  4. ⇒ v = -60025
  5. v = -24 cm
  6. Finally 115 = 1v1 - 120
  7. ⇒ -115 + 120 = 1v1
  8. ⇒ v1 = 3005
  9. So image is displaced by 36 cm away from mirror (d)
steps: $\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{q}$
$\Rightarrow -\frac{1}{15} = \frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{40}$
$\Rightarrow \frac{1}{v} = -\frac{1}{15} + \frac{1}{40}$
$\Rightarrow v = \frac{-600}{25}$
$v = -24\,\mathrm{cm}$
Finally $\frac{1}{15} = \frac{1}{v^{1}} - \frac{1}{20}$
$\Rightarrow -\frac{1}{15} + \frac{1}{20} = \frac{1}{v^{1}}$
$\Rightarrow v^{1} = \frac{300}{5}$
So image is displaced by $36\,\mathrm{cm}$ away from mirror (d)
printed_lines: So image is displaced by 36 cm away from mirror (d)

steps: Use the mirror formula $\frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}$ with $f = -15\,\mathrm{cm}$ (concave).
Initial position $u_1 = -40\,\mathrm{cm}$: $\frac{1}{v_1} = -\frac{1}{15} + \frac{1}{40} = \frac{-8+3}{120} = -\frac{1}{24}$, so $v_1 = -24\,\mathrm{cm}$.
Object moved $20\,\mathrm{cm}$ towards the mirror: $u_2 = -20\,\mathrm{cm}$.
The image shifts from $24\,\mathrm{cm}$ to $60\,\mathrm{cm}$ in front of the mirror: $|\Delta v| = 60 - 24 = 36\,\mathrm{cm}$ away from the mirror, which is option $4$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Use the mirror formula 1v + 1u = 1f with f = -15 cm (concave).
  2. Initial position u1 = -40 cm: 1v1 = -115 + 140 = -8+3120 = -124, so v1 = -24 cm.
  3. Object moved 20 cm towards the mirror: u2 = -20 cm.
  4. 1v2 = -115 + 120 = -4+360 = -160, so v2 = -60 cm.
  5. The image shifts from 24 cm to 60 cm in front of the mirror: |Δ v| = 60 - 24 = 36 cm away from the mirror, which is option 4.
ai_solution.why: Mirror formula: image moves from 24 cm to 60 cm in front of the mirror, i.e. 36 cm away from the mirror.

chapter.name: Ray Optics
chapter.why: The answer turns on applying the mirror equation for a concave mirror (image moves from 24 cm to 60 cm, i.e. 36 cm away from the mirror), which is ray optics.

subtopics.name: Mirror Equation
subtopics.why: The answer comes from applying the mirror equation 1/v + 1/u = 1/f to a concave mirror (f = -15 cm) at u = -40 cm (v = -24 cm) and u = -20 cm (v = -60 cm), so the image moves 36 cm away from the mirror.

step_list: apply the mirror formula with sign convention (u = -40 cm, f = -15 cm) to find the initial image distance
take the new object distance (u = -20 cm after moving 20 cm towards the mirror) and apply the mirror formula again for the new image distance
subtract the two image distances and read the direction of the image shift from the signs
difficulty.why: Two applications of the mirror formula at the two object positions, then a signed difference to get both the size and the direction of the image shift.
difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: Options come in towards/away pairs with the same magnitude, so a sign-convention slip in reading the direction picks the wrong one of the pair.

The object came 20 cm closer, so the image also moves 36 cm closer.
steps.fix: Compare the two numbers: 60 cm is farther out than 24 cm, so the image recedes 36 cm as the object approaches the focus.

other_options.proof: 30 cm is not reachable from the printed numbers. The two image distances are fixed at 24 cm and 60 cm under either sign convention, so the answer is 36 cm; I then substituted the usual slips and none lands on 30 cm -- $v=uf/(u+f)$ gives 10.9 cm and 8.6 cm, a difference of 2.3 cm; taking $f$ as $R/2=7.5\,\mathrm{cm}$ gives 9.2 cm and 12 cm, a difference of 2.8 cm; scaling the 20 cm by the magnification $(v/u)^2$ gives 7.2 cm; and moving the object 20 cm the other way gives 4 cm. 30 cm is the second magnitude of a two-by-two grid of 30 and 36 crossed with towards and away.

Same arithmetic as option 2: 30 cm is reached by no substitution into the mirror equation with $f=15\,\mathrm{cm}$, $u=40\,\mathrm{cm}$ and $u=20\,\mathrm{cm}$, and this option carries the wrong direction as well, so it is the fourth cell of the 30/36 by towards/away grid.

question.stem: An em wave is propagating in a medium with a velocity $\vec{V} = V\hat{i}$. The instantaneous oscillating electric field of this em wave is along $+y$ axis. Then the direction of oscillating magnetic field of the em wave will be along

solution.full_text:
1. Direction of propagation of Em wave is same as $\vec{E} \times \vec{B}$
2. So, $\hat{i} = \hat{j} \times (B)$
3. So direction of $B$ is along $k$
solution.html:
1. Direction of propagation of Em wave is same as →E × →B
  2. So, ˆı = ˆȷ × (B)
  3. So direction of B is along k
steps: Direction of propagation of Em wave is same as $\vec{E} \times \vec{B}$
So, $\hat{i} = \hat{j} \times (B)$
So direction of $B$ is along $k$
printed_lines: Direction of propagation of Em wave is same as

steps: An em wave travels along $\vec{E} \times \vec{B}$, so $\hat{E} \times \hat{B} = \hat{V} = \hat{i}$.
With $\hat{E} = \hat{j}$, we need $\hat{j} \times \hat{B} = \hat{i}$.
Since $\hat{j} \times \hat{k} = \hat{i}$, $\hat{B} = +\hat{k}$, i.e. the $+z$ direction, which is option $4$.

  3. Since ˆȷ × ˆk = ˆı, ˆB = +ˆk, i.e. the +z direction, which is option 4.
ai_solution.why: The wave travels along E x B; with E along +y and propagation along +x, B must be along +z because y-hat x z-hat = x-hat.

chapter.name: Electromagnetic Waves
chapter.why: The answer turns on the transverse nature of a plane em wave, where E x B points along the propagation direction, so with propagation along +x and E along +y the magnetic field must be along +z.

subtopics.name: Transverse Nature of Electromagnetic Waves
subtopics.why: The answer depends on E and B oscillating perpendicular to each other and to the propagation direction, with E x B along the velocity (+x), so with E along +y the field B must be along +z.

step_list: Recall that for an em wave E, B and the propagation direction are mutually perpendicular with E x B along the velocity
Apply the cross product with E along +y and propagation along +x (j x ? = i) to fix the sign and axis of B
difficulty.why: The work is one recall (E x B points along propagation) followed by one unit-vector cross-product application to find B's axis and sign.
difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: The -z option is exactly what results from taking B x E instead of E x B (reversed order), so a candidate unsure of the order lands on a listed distractor.

categories.concept: In an electromagnetic wave $\vec E$, $\vec B$ and the direction of travel form a right-handed set in that order, so $\hat B = \hat v \times \hat E$

trap.label: reversed
trap.route: The right triad is used but in the other order -- $\hat E \times \hat v = \hat j \times \hat i = -\hat k$ -- which turns the answer round to $-z$
trap.who: a student who has learnt that $\vec E$, $\vec B$ and $\vec v$ are mutually perpendicular and right-handed, but has not fixed which two vectors are crossed to get the third
trap.feels: the magnitude of the cross product is right, the axis is right, and $-z$ is what comes out of a cross product of the two vectors the stem actually names

steps.text: $\vec E$ is along $+y$ and the wave travels along $+x$, so $\vec B$ must lie along the $z$ axis.
Cross the two given directions in the order they are given: $\hat j \times \hat i = -\hat k$, so $\vec B$ is along $-z$.
steps.fix: The ordered set is $\vec E \times \vec B$ along the travel direction, so $\hat j \times \hat B = \hat i$ requires $\hat B = +\hat k$.

other_options.who: a student who remembers that the electric and magnetic fields of an em wave rise and fall together along the same wavefront and pictures them on the same line
other_options.feels: $-y$ is the one option that keeps $\vec B$ in step with the $+y$ electric field, which matches the half-remembered 'in phase' statement

steps.text: $\vec E$ and $\vec B$ oscillate in phase in an em wave.
So $\vec B$ lies along the same axis as $\vec E$, pointing the other way during the cycle: $-y$.
steps.fix: In phase means their magnitudes peak together; their directions stay perpendicular, so $\vec B$ cannot lie on the $y$ axis at all.

other_options.proof: $-x$ is along the propagation direction the stem prints as $\vec V = V\hat i$, and an em wave is transverse, so no route that keeps the three vectors mutually perpendicular can put $\vec B$ on the $x$ axis. I also checked the two sign slips available on this question -- crossing in the wrong order, and reversing the right-hand rule -- and both land on $\pm z$, never on $\pm x$.

steps: The ray retraces its path only if it strikes the silvered face along the normal, so the angle of incidence on that face is $r_2 = 0^\circ$.
For a prism $r_1 + r_2 = A$, so $r_1 = A - 0^\circ = 30^\circ$.
Snell's law at the first face: $\sin i = \mu \sin r_1 = \sqrt{2} \times \sin 30^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$.
$i = \sin^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) = 45^\circ$, which is option $4$.
ai_solution.html:
1. The ray retraces its path only if it strikes the silvered face along the normal, so the angle of incidence on that face is r2 = 0°.
  2. For a prism r1 + r2 = A, so r1 = A - 0° = 30°.
  3. Snell's law at the first face: sin i = μ sin r1 = 2 × sin 30° = 22 = 12.
  4. i = sin-1(12) = 45°, which is option 4.
ai_solution.why: To retrace its path the ray must hit the silvered face normally, so the refraction angle at the first face is r = A = 30 degrees; sin i = sqrt(2) sin 30 = 1/sqrt(2), so i = 45 degrees.

subtopics.name: Prism
subtopics.why: The answer depends on prism geometry: to retrace its path the ray must strike the silvered face normally, so the refraction angle at the first face equals the prism angle (r = A = 30 degrees), giving sin i = sqrt(2) sin 30 degrees, so i = 45 degrees.

step_list: recognise that retracing the path requires the ray to strike the silvered face along the normal, so the refraction angle at that face is r2 = 0
use the prism relation r1 + r2 = A to get the refraction angle at the entry face, r1 = 30 degrees
apply Snell's law at the entry face, sin i = sqrt(2) x sin 30 degrees, to get the angle of incidence
difficulty.why: The work is turning 'retraces its path' into normal incidence on the mirrored face, then using r1 + r2 = A and one Snell's-law substitution with a standard surd value.
difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: Two options are the results of wrong routes: 30 degrees is r1 reported as the incidence angle (skipping Snell's law), and zero comes from putting the normal-incidence condition on the entry face instead of the silvered face.

trap.feels: $30^{\circ}$ is the one angle the stem prints, and it is a genuine angle in the solved ray diagram, so it reads like the answer already found

steps.text: To retrace, the ray must hit the silvered face normally, so inside the glass it makes $30^{\circ}$ with the normal of the entry face.
So the angle of incidence is $30^{\circ}$.
steps.fix: That $30^{\circ}$ is the angle INSIDE the glass; $\sin i = \sqrt2 \sin 30^{\circ} = 0.707$ gives $i = 45^{\circ}$ outside.

other_options.who: a student who has learnt 'a ray retraces its path when it meets a mirror along the normal' and applies it to the face the light enters through
other_options.feels: the stem's condition is retracing, and zero incidence is the textbook condition for a ray to come straight back, so 'Zero' answers the remembered rule exactly

steps.text: Retracing needs normal incidence on the reflecting surface.
So the beam must enter the prism at zero incidence.
steps.fix: The silvered surface is the OTHER face; at zero incidence on the entry face the ray would meet the silvered face at $30^{\circ}$, not along its normal.

other_options.who: a student who remembers the result that a prism with one face silvered behaves like a prism of twice the angle and uses that doubling in place of Snell's law
other_options.feels: the light does cross the glass twice, so doubling the $30^{\circ}$ prism angle feels like the step that accounts for the second pass, and $60^{\circ}$ is then the only angle in the list built from the stem's own number

steps.text: The silvered face sends the beam back through the prism, so the path is traversed twice.
So the effective angle is $2A = 60^{\circ}$ and that is the angle of incidence.
steps.fix: Doubling describes the deviation of a silvered prism, not the incidence angle; the incidence angle still comes from $\sin i = n\sin A$.

solution.full_text:
1. Due to heating, number of electron-hole pairs will increase,  so overall resistance of diode will change.
2. Due to which forward biasing and reversed biasing both are charged.
solution.html:
1. Due to heating, number of electron-hole pairs will increase, so overall resistance of diode will change.
  2. Due to which forward biasing and reversed biasing both are charged.
steps: Due to heating, number of electron-hole pairs will increase,  so overall resistance of diode will change.
Due to which forward biasing and reversed biasing both are charged.
printed_lines: 6. Due to heating, number of electron-hole pairs will increase,  so overall resistance of diode
Due to which forward biasing and reversed biasing both are charged.

steps: Heating increases thermal generation of electron-hole pairs, so the minority-carrier concentration $n_i^2 \propto T^3 e^{-E_g/kT}$ rises.
In reverse bias, the reverse saturation current $I_0$ rises with $T$, so the reverse resistance falls.
In forward bias, the barrier potential $V_0$ (knee voltage) falls with rising $T$, so the forward current at a given $V$ rises and the forward resistance falls.
Since both forward and reverse parts change, temperature affects the overall $V$-$I$ characteristics, which is option $1$.

  2. In reverse bias, the reverse saturation current I0 rises with T, so the reverse resistance falls.
  3. In forward bias, the barrier potential V0 (knee voltage) falls with rising T, so the forward current at a given V rises and the forward resistance falls.
  4. Since both forward and reverse parts change, temperature affects the overall V-I characteristics, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: Heating raises the number of thermally generated minority carriers and lowers the barrier potential, so both forward and reverse behaviour change: the whole V-I characteristic shifts.

question.full_text:
The power radiated by a black body is $P$ and it radiates maximum energy at wavelength, $\lambda_0$ If the temperature of the black body is now changes so that it radiates maximum energy at wavelength $\frac{3}{4}\lambda_0$, the power radiated by it becomes $nP$. The value of $n$ is
(1) $\frac{81}{256}$
(2) $\frac{3}{4}$
(3) $\frac{256}{81}$
(4) $\frac{4}{3}$
question.html:
The power radiated by a black body is P and it radiates maximum energy at wavelength, λ0 If the temperature of the black body is now changes so that it radiates maximum energy at wavelength 34λ0, the power radiated by it becomes nP. The value of n is
  1. (1)81256
  2. (2)34
  3. (3)25681
  4. (4)43
question.stem: The power radiated by a black body is $P$ and it radiates maximum energy at wavelength, $\lambda_0$ If the temperature of the black body is now changes so that it radiates maximum energy at wavelength $\frac{3}{4}\lambda_0$, the power radiated by it becomes $nP$. The value of $n$ is

solution.full_text:
1. We know, $\lambda_{\max}\,T = \text{constant}$ (wien's law)
2. So, $\lambda_{\max 1}T_1 = \lambda_{\max 2}T_2$
3. $\Rightarrow \lambda_0 T = \frac{3\lambda_0}{4}T'$
4. $\Rightarrow T' = \frac{4}{3}T$
5. So, $\frac{P_2}{P_1} = \left(\frac{T'}{T}\right)^{4} = \left(\frac{4}{3}\right)^{4} = \frac{256}{81}$
solution.html:
1. We know, λmax T = constant (wien's law)
  2. So, λmax 1T1 = λmax 2T2
  3. ⇒ λ0 T = 3λ04T'
  4. ⇒ T' = 43T
  5. So, P2P1 = (T'T)4 = (43)4 = 25681
steps: We know, $\lambda_{\max}\,T = \text{constant}$ (wien's law)
So, $\lambda_{\max 1}T_1 = \lambda_{\max 2}T_2$
$\Rightarrow \lambda_0 T = \frac{3\lambda_0}{4}T'$
$\Rightarrow T' = \frac{4}{3}T$
So, $\frac{P_2}{P_1} = \left(\frac{T'}{T}\right)^{4} = \left(\frac{4}{3}\right)^{4} = \frac{256}{81}$
By Wien's displacement law, $\lambda_m T = \text{constant}$, so $\lambda_0 T = \frac{3}{4}\lambda_0 T'$.
Hence $T' = \frac{4}{3}T$.
By Stefan's law, $P \propto T^4$, so $\frac{nP}{P} = \left(\frac{T'}{T}\right)^4$.
$n = \left(\frac{4}{3}\right)^4 = \frac{256}{81}$, which is option $3$.
ai_solution.html:
1. By Wien's displacement law, λm T = constant, so λ0 T = 34λ0 T'.
  2. Hence T' = 43T.
  3. By Stefan's law, P ∝ T4, so nPP = (T'T)4.
  4. n = (43)4 = 25681, which is option 3.
ai_solution.why: Wien's law gives T' = (4/3)T when lambda_max becomes (3/4)lambda_0; Stefan's law P proportional to T^4 gives n = (4/3)^4 = 256/81.

question.stem: A small sphere of radius ‘$r$’ falls from rest in a viscous liquid. AS a result is produced due to viscous force, The rate of production of heat when the sphere attains its terminal velocity, is proportional to

solution.full_text:
1. Rate of prod of heat $= F \times u$
2. $= 6\pi n r v \times v$
3. $= 6\pi n r\left[\frac{2}{9}\frac{r^{2}g}{n}\left(p_{b} - p_{l}\right)\right]$
4. So, Rate of prod of heat $\times r^{5}$

1. Rate of prod of heat = F × u
  2. = 6π n r v × v
  3. = 6π n r[29r2gn(pb - pl)]
  4. So, Rate of prod of heat × r5

$= 6\pi n r v \times v$
$= 6\pi n r\left[\frac{2}{9}\frac{r^{2}g}{n}\left(p_{b} - p_{l}\right)\right]$
So, Rate of prod of heat $\times r^{5}$

steps: At terminal velocity the net force is zero, giving $v_t = \frac{2 r^{2} (\rho - \sigma) g}{9 \eta}$, so $v_t \propto r^{2}$.
The viscous force is $F = 6 \pi \eta r v_t$, so $F \propto r \cdot r^{2} = r^{3}$.
The rate of heat production equals the power against viscosity, $P = F v_t$.
$P \propto r^{3} \cdot r^{2} = r^{5}$, which is option $3$.

  3. The rate of heat production equals the power against viscosity, P = F vt.
  4. P ∝ r3 · r2 = r5, which is option 3.
ai_solution.why: At terminal velocity v is proportional to r^2, viscous force F = 6*pi*eta*r*v is proportional to r^3, so heat rate P = F*v is proportional to r^5.

1. Accd to Ensein’s Eq,
  2. h × 2v0 = w0 + 12nv12 .....(1)
  3. & h × 5v0 = w0 + 12nv12 .....(2)
  4. Since w0 = hv0
  5. From (1), hv0 = 12mv12
  6. & From (2) h × 4v0 = 12mv22
  7. ⇒ 4 = v22v12

steps: Accd to Ensein’s Eq,
Since $w_0 = hv_0$
& From (2) $h \times 4v_0 = \frac{1}{2}mv_2^{2}$
$\Rightarrow 4 = \frac{v_2^{2}}{v_1^{2}}$
$\Rightarrow \frac{v_2}{v_1} = 2$
Einstein's photoelectric equation: $\frac{1}{2}mv_{max}^2 = h\nu - h\nu_0$.
Dividing: $\frac{v_1^2}{v_2^2} = \frac{h\nu_0}{4h\nu_0} = \frac{1}{4}$.
$\frac{v_1}{v_2} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{4}} = \frac{1}{2}$, so $v_1 : v_2 = 1 : 2$, which is option $2$.

  4. Dividing: v12v22 = hν04hν0 = 14.
  5. v1v2 = 14 = 12, so v1 : v2 = 1 : 2, which is option 2.

6. $\Rightarrow 150 = 600 \times \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{1}$
7. $\Rightarrow$ No of half lives $= 2$

Get the velocity at time t from v = V0 + (eE0/m)t

trap.feels: the bracket $\left(1+\frac{eE_0}{mV_0}t\right)$ is exactly the expression the student has just derived, and seeing it written out beside $\lambda_0$ makes the option look like the finished line of working

steps.text: The force on the electron is $+eE_0\hat i$, so $v = v_0 + (eE_0/m)t$ and the momentum grows by the factor $1 + eE_0t/mv_0$.
So the wavelength grows by the same factor: $\lambda_0\left(1+\frac{eE_0}{mV_0}t\right)$.
steps.fix: $\lambda = h/p$: when the momentum is multiplied by a factor the wavelength is DIVIDED by it.

other_options.proof: An unchanged $\lambda_0$ requires an unchanged momentum, and the stem puts a charge $-e$ in a field $-E_0\hat i$ along the line of motion, which gives a force of $eE_0$ with no transverse component. The one sign slip available here -- forgetting that the electron's charge is negative -- flips the force and gives $\lambda_0/(1-eE_0t/mv_0)$, which is still not $\lambda_0$; reaching $\lambda_0$ needs the force to be zero, which no reading of the printed vectors supplies.

$\lambda_0 t$ is a length multiplied by a time, so it cannot be a wavelength at all; it is the only option that is not $\lambda_0$ times a dimensionless factor. A dimensional check kills it without any physics, and no rearrangement of $\lambda = h/(mv_0 + eE_0t)$ produces a term linear in $t$ outside the denominator.

question.full_text:
The ratio of kinetic energy to the total energy of an electron in a Bohr orbit of the hydrogen atom is:
(1) $1 : -2$
(2) $1 : 1$
(3) $2 : -1$
(4) $1 : -1$
question.html:
The ratio of kinetic energy to the total energy of an electron in a Bohr orbit of the hydrogen atom is:
  1. (1)1 : -2
  2. (2)1 : 1
  3. (3)2 : -1
  4. (4)1 : -1
question.stem: The ratio of kinetic energy to the total energy of an electron in a Bohr orbit of the hydrogen atom is:

solution.full_text:
1. Since, Total energy $= -$ (Kinetic energy)
2. So, $\frac{\text{k.e}}{\text{t.e}}\ 1 : -1$
solution.html:
1. Since, Total energy = - (Kinetic energy)
  2. So, k.et.e 1 : -1
steps: Since, Total energy $= -$ (Kinetic energy)
So, $\frac{\text{k.e}}{\text{t.e}}\ 1 : -1$
In a Bohr orbit the centripetal force is the Coulomb force: $\frac{mv^2}{r} = \frac{kZe^2}{r^2}$.
So the kinetic energy is $K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{kZe^2}{2r}$.
The potential energy is $U = -\frac{kZe^2}{r} = -2K$.
The total energy is $E = K + U = K - 2K = -K$.
Hence $K : E = K : (-K) = 1 : -1$, which is option $4$.
ai_solution.html:
1. In a Bohr orbit the centripetal force is the Coulomb force: mv2r = kZe2r2.
  2. So the kinetic energy is K = 12mv2 = kZe22r.
  3. The potential energy is U = -kZe2r = -2K.
  4. The total energy is E = K + U = K - 2K = -K.
  5. Hence K : E = K : (-K) = 1 : -1, which is option 4.
ai_solution.why: In a Bohr orbit KE = -E (total energy), so KE : E = 1 : -1.

question.full_text:
A tuning fork is used to produced resonance in glass tube. The length of the air column in the tube can be adjusted by a variable piston. A room temperature of $27^{0}\,\mathrm{C}$ two successive resonances are produced at $20\,\mathrm{cm}$ and $73\,\mathrm{cm}$ column length. If the frequency of the tuning for is $320\,\mathrm{Hz}$, The velocity of sound in air at $27^{0}\,\mathrm{C}$ is
(1) $300\,\mathrm{m/s}$
(2) $330\,\mathrm{m/s}$
(3) $350\,\mathrm{m/s}$
(4) $339\,\mathrm{m/s}$
question.html:
A tuning fork is used to produced resonance in glass tube. The length of the air column in the tube can be adjusted by a variable piston. A room temperature of 270 C two successive resonances are produced at 20 cm and 73 cm column length. If the frequency of the tuning for is 320 Hz, The velocity of sound in air at 270 C is
  1. (1)300 m/s
  2. (2)330 m/s
  3. (3)350 m/s
  4. (4)339 m/s
question.stem: A tuning fork is used to produced resonance in glass tube. The length of the air column in the tube can be adjusted by a variable piston. A room temperature of $27^{0}\,\mathrm{C}$ two successive resonances are produced at $20\,\mathrm{cm}$ and $73\,\mathrm{cm}$ column length. If the frequency of the tuning for is $320\,\mathrm{Hz}$, The velocity of sound in air at $27^{0}\,\mathrm{C}$ is

solution.full_text:
1. This is a closed pipe
2. Atv, $320 = \frac{v}{4\{20 + e} = \frac{3v}{4[73 + e]}$
3. $E$ = end correction
4. $\Rightarrow 73 + e = 60 + 3e$
5. $\Rightarrow e = \frac{13}{2}\,\mathrm{cm} = 6.5\,\mathrm{cm}$
6. So, $320 = = \frac{v}{4 \times \left(\frac{26.5}{100}\right)}$
7. $\Rightarrow v = 320 \times 4 \times \frac{26.5}{100} = 339\,\mathrm{m/s}$
solution.html:
1. This is a closed pipe
  2. Atv, 320 = v4{20 + e = 3v4[73 + e]
  3. E = end correction
  4. ⇒ 73 + e = 60 + 3e
  5. ⇒ e = 132 cm = 6.5 cm
  6. So, 320 = = v4 × (26.5100)
  7. ⇒ v = 320 × 4 × 26.5100 = 339 m/s
steps: This is a closed pipe
$E$ = end correction
$\Rightarrow 73 + e = 60 + 3e$
$\Rightarrow e = \frac{13}{2}\,\mathrm{cm} = 6.5\,\mathrm{cm}$
So, $320 = = \frac{v}{4 \times \left(\frac{26.5}{100}\right)}$
$\Rightarrow v = 320 \times 4 \times \frac{26.5}{100} = 339\,\mathrm{m/s}$
For a resonance tube, two successive resonance lengths differ by half a wavelength: $l_2 - l_1 = \frac{\lambda}{2}$.
$\frac{\lambda}{2} = 73\,\mathrm{cm} - 20\,\mathrm{cm} = 53\,\mathrm{cm}$.
$\lambda = 2 \times 53\,\mathrm{cm} = 106\,\mathrm{cm} = 1.06\,\mathrm{m}$.
$v = f\lambda = 320\,\mathrm{Hz} \times 1.06\,\mathrm{m} = 339.2\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
$339.2\,\mathrm{m/s} \approx 339\,\mathrm{m/s}$, which is option $4$.
ai_solution.html:
1. For a resonance tube, two successive resonance lengths differ by half a wavelength: l2 - l1 = λ2.
  2. λ2 = 73 cm - 20 cm = 53 cm.
  3. λ = 2 × 53 cm = 106 cm = 1.06 m.
  4. v = fλ = 320 Hz × 1.06 m = 339.2 m/s.
  5. 339.2 m/s ≈ 339 m/s, which is option 4.
ai_solution.why: Successive resonances differ by lambda/2: lambda = 2(73-20) cm = 1.06 m, so v = 320 x 1.06 = 339.2 m/s, which is about 339 m/s.

The electron has charge $-e$, so an upward field $E$ pushes it downward with force $F = eE$; gravity is negligible beside this force.
Electron acceleration: $a_e = \frac{eE}{m_e}$.
With the field reversed (downward), the proton of charge $+e$ is also pushed downward: $a_p = \frac{eE}{m_p}$.
Falling from rest, $h = \frac{1}{2} a t^2$, so $t = \sqrt{\frac{2h}{a}} = \sqrt{\frac{2hm}{eE}}$, i.e. $t \propto \sqrt{m}$.
$\frac{t_e}{t_p} = \sqrt{\frac{m_e}{m_p}} \ll 1$, so the electron's time of fall is smaller, which is option $2$.

  4. Falling from rest, h = 12 a t2, so t = 2ha = 2hmeE, i.e. t ∝ m.
  5. tetp = memp ≪ 1, so the electron's time of fall is smaller, which is option 2.
ai_solution.why: Each particle gets acceleration eE/m (gravity negligible), so t = sqrt(2hm/(eE)) is proportional to sqrt(m); the electron's much smaller mass makes its fall time smaller.

steps: Acceleration due to gravity on the Earth is $g = \frac{G M_e}{R_e^2}$, which involves $G$ and the Earth's mass, not the sun's mass.

Hence the statement '$g$ on the Earth will not change' is not correct (option $1$).
Larger $g$ makes raindrops fall faster, so option $2$ is correct.

The only incorrect statement is option $1$.

$\omega = \frac{L}{I}$ decreases as $I$ increases, so angular velocity is not constant.
$K = \frac{L^2}{2I}$ decreases as $I$ increases, so rotational kinetic energy is not constant.

  5. K = L22I decreases as I increases, so rotational kinetic energy is not constant.
  6. Only angular momentum stays constant, which is option 1.

question.full_text:
A then diamagnetic rod is placed vertically between the poles of an electromagnet when the current in the electromagnet is switched on, then the diamagnetic rod is pushed up, out of the horizontal magnetic field, Hence the rod gains gravitational potential energy. The work required to do this comes from.
(1) the induced electric field due to the changing magnectic field
(2) the current source
(3) the lattice structure of the material of the rod
(4) the magnetic field
question.html:

The work required to do this comes from.
  1. (1)the induced electric field due to the changing magnectic field
  2. (2)the current source
  3. (3)the lattice structure of the material of the rod
  4. (4)the magnetic field
question.stem: A then diamagnetic rod is placed vertically between the poles of an electromagnet when the current in the electromagnet is switched on, then the diamagnetic rod is pushed up, out of the horizontal magnetic field, Hence the rod gains gravitational potential energy. The work required to do this comes from.

options.text: the induced electric field due to the changing magnectic field
the lattice structure of the material of the rod

answer.publisher_text: the induced electric field due to the changing magnectic field

solution.full_text: 1. Because when electromagnet is switched in the magnetic field associated with rod increases and leads to generation of induced electric field.
solution.html: 1. Because when electromagnet is switched in the magnetic field associated with rod increases and leads to generation of induced electric field.
steps: Because when electromagnet is switched in the magnetic field associated with rod increases and leads to generation of induced electric field.
printed_lines: Because when electromagnet is switched in the magnetic field associated with rod increases
and leads to generation of induced electric field.

steps: When the current is switched on, the electromagnet's field is set up by the external current source, which does work against the back-emf.
The diamagnetic rod is repelled from the strong-field region and rises, gaining gravitational potential energy $\Delta U = mgh$.
As the rod moves, the flux linkage of the coil changes, inducing an emf that the current source must work against; the extra work it does supplies $mgh$.
The magnetic field only stores and transfers energy, and the lattice and induced electric field are not energy sources, so the work comes from the current source, which is option $2$.
ai_solution.html:

  2. The diamagnetic rod is repelled from the strong-field region and rises, gaining gravitational potential energy Δ U = mgh.
  3. As the rod moves, the flux linkage of the coil changes, inducing an emf that the current source must work against; the extra work it does supplies mgh.
  4. The magnetic field only stores and transfers energy, and the lattice and induced electric field are not energy sources, so the work comes from the current source, which is option 2.
ai_solution.why: The energy to push the rod up is ultimately supplied by the current source that drives the electromagnet; the field only stores and transfers that energy.

chapter.name: Electromagnetic Induction
chapter.why: The answer turns on the induced electric field produced by a changing magnetic field (Faraday's law) doing the work on a diamagnetic rod, which needs both electromagnetic induction and diamagnetism.

subtopics.name: Induced Electric Field
subtopics.why: The answer is that the work comes from the induced electric field produced by the changing magnetic field when the electromagnet is switched on.

step_list: Recall that a diamagnetic material is repelled from the strong-field region, which is why the rod is pushed up out of the field

Recognise that the magnetic field is only the agent that transmits the force and is not itself a reservoir of energy that can supply net work (a static magnetic field does no net work), and that the induced electric field and the rod's lattice are not energy sources here
Use energy conservation to trace the gain in gravitational potential energy back through the field to the external agent that sets up and maintains the field, and pick that option
difficulty.why: The work is a conceptual energy-accounting chain: recall diamagnetic repulsion, rule out the field and the rod's own material as energy sources, then follow energy conservation back to what powers the electromagnet.
difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: The option 'the magnetic field' is exactly the result of the plausible wrong route of assuming that whatever exerts the force supplies the energy; seeing past it needs the non-obvious insight that the field only transfers energy from its source. The energy accounting (back-emf work done by the supply as the rod's magnetisation changes the flux) is not worked through in NCERT's Magnetism and Matter chapter.

question.full_text:
Current sensitivity of a moving coil galvanometer is $5\,\mathrm{div/Ma}$ and its voltage sensitivity (angular deflection per unit voltage applied) is $20\,\mathrm{div/V}$. The resistance of the galvanometer is
(1) $500\,\Omega$
(2) $40\,\Omega$
(3) $250\,\Omega$
(4) $25\,\Omega$

solution.full_text:
1. $R = \frac{\text{Voltage Sensitivity}}{\text{Current Sensitivity}}\frac{(\mathrm{V/div})}{(\mathrm{A/div})}$
2. $= \frac{\frac{1}{20}}{\frac{1}{5000}} = 250\,\mathrm{ohm}$
solution.html:
1. R = Voltage SensitivityCurrent Sensitivity(V/div)(A/div)
  2. = 12015000 = 250 ohm
steps: $R = \frac{\text{Voltage Sensitivity}}{\text{Current Sensitivity}}\frac{(\mathrm{V/div})}{(\mathrm{A/div})}$
Current sensitivity $I_s = \frac{\theta}{I} = 5\,\mathrm{div/mA} = 5000\,\mathrm{div/A}$.
Voltage sensitivity $V_s = \frac{\theta}{V} = \frac{\theta}{I G} = \frac{I_s}{G}$.
$G = \frac{I_s}{V_s} = \frac{5000\,\mathrm{div/A}}{20\,\mathrm{div/V}} = 250\,\Omega$, which is option $3$.

  2. Voltage sensitivity Vs = θV = θI G = IsG.
  3. G = IsVs = 5000 div/A20 div/V = 250 Ω, which is option 3.
ai_solution.why: R = current sensitivity / voltage sensitivity = (5000 div/A)/(20 div/V) = 250 ohm.

$\mathrm{Vol} \times \mathrm{temp}$
So pressure = constent

The $V$-$T$ graph is a straight line through the origin, so $V \propto T$ and the process A to B is isobaric ($P$ constant).

5. $\Rightarrow T \approx 8.36\times10^{4}\,\mathrm{K}$

question.full_text:
Unpolarised light is incident from air on a plane surface of a material of refractive index ‘$\mu$’ At a particular angle of incidence ‘I’, it is found that the reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular to each other, Which of the following options is correct for this situation?
(1) $i = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{\mu}\right)$
(2) Reflected light is polarized with its electric vector parallel to the plane of incidence
(3) $i = \sin^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{\mu}\right)$
(4) Reflected light is polarized with its electric vector perpendicular to the plane of incidence
question.html:
Unpolarised light is incident from air on a plane surface of a material of refractive index ‘μ’ At a particular angle of incidence ‘I’, it is found that the reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular to each other, Which of the following options is correct for this situation?
  1. (1)i = tan-1(1μ)
  2. (2)Reflected light is polarized with its electric vector parallel to the plane of incidence
  3. (3)i = sin-1(1μ)
  4. (4)Reflected light is polarized with its electric vector perpendicular to the plane of incidence

Reflected light is polarized with its electric vector perpendicular to the plane of incidence

answer.publisher_text: Reflected light is polarized with its electric vector perpendicular to the plane of incidence

solution.full_text:
1. Since reflected & refracted rays are mutually perp
2. So, $\mu = \tan (i)$
3. So, Ans (4)
solution.html:
1. Since reflected & refracted rays are mutually perp
  2. So, μ = tan (i)
  3. So, Ans (4)
steps: Since reflected & refracted rays are mutually perp
So, $\mu = \tan (i)$
So, Ans (4)
printed_lines: Since reflected & refracted rays are mutually perp

steps: Reflected and refracted rays perpendicular means $i + r = 90^\circ$, so $r = 90^\circ - i$.
Snell's law: $\sin i = \mu \sin r = \mu \sin(90^\circ - i) = \mu \cos i$.
Hence $\tan i = \mu$, i.e. $i = \tan^{-1}\mu$ (Brewster angle), so options $1$ ($\tan^{-1}(1/\mu)$) and $3$ ($\sin^{-1}(1/\mu)$) are wrong.
At the Brewster angle the component with $\vec{E}$ parallel to the plane of incidence is not reflected, so option $2$ is wrong.
The reflected light is plane polarized with $\vec{E}$ perpendicular to the plane of incidence, which is option $4$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Reflected and refracted rays perpendicular means i + r = 90°, so r = 90° - i.
  2. Snell's law: sin i = μ sin r = μ sin(90° - i) = μ cos i.
  3. Hence tan i = μ, i.e. i = tan-1μ (Brewster angle), so options 1 (tan-1(1/μ)) and 3 (sin-1(1/μ)) are wrong.
  4. At the Brewster angle the component with →E parallel to the plane of incidence is not reflected, so option 2 is wrong.
  5. The reflected light is plane polarized with →E perpendicular to the plane of incidence, which is option 4.
ai_solution.why: Reflected and refracted rays perpendicular means incidence at Brewster angle (tan i = mu), where the reflected light is fully polarized with its electric vector perpendicular to the plane of incidence.

3. & $0.21 = \frac{\lambda}{d^{1}}$

steps: For telescope
$M = \frac{f_o}{f_e}$

For a refracting telescope in normal adjustment, $m = \frac{f_o}{f_e}$, so a large objective focal length $f_o$ gives large angular magnification.
The minimum resolvable angle is $\Delta\theta = \frac{1.22\,\lambda}{D}$, so resolving power $\frac{1}{\Delta\theta} = \frac{D}{1.22\,\lambda}$ increases with objective diameter $D$.
Both conditions together need large focal length and large diameter, which is option $3$.

solution.full_text:
1. For body to complete vertical circle
2. $V_A = \sqrt{5Rg} = \sqrt{\frac{5}{2}gD}$
3. So, $\sqrt{2gH} = \sqrt{\frac{5}{2}gD}$
4. $\Rightarrow 2gH = \frac{5}{2}\cancel{g}D$
5. $\Rightarrow H = \frac{5}{4}D$
solution.html:
1. For body to complete vertical circle
  2. VA = 5Rg = 52gD
  3. So, 2gH = 52gD
  4. ⇒ 2gH = 52gD
  5. ⇒ H = 54D
steps: For body to complete vertical circle
$V_A = \sqrt{5Rg} = \sqrt{\frac{5}{2}gD}$
So, $\sqrt{2gH} = \sqrt{\frac{5}{2}gD}$
$\Rightarrow 2gH = \frac{5}{2}\cancel{g}D$
$\Rightarrow H = \frac{5}{4}D$
printed_lines: For body to complete vertical circle

steps: The circle has diameter $AB = D$, so its radius is $R = \frac{D}{2}$.
To just complete the vertical circle, the speed at the top $B$ must satisfy $v_B^2 = gR$ (normal force zero there).
Energy conservation from $A$ to $B$: $v_A^2 = v_B^2 + 2g(2R) = gR + 4gR = 5gR$.
Energy conservation on the frictionless track from rest at height $h$ to $A$: $mgh = \frac{1}{2}m v_A^2 = \frac{5}{2}mgR$, so $h = \frac{5}{2}R$.
$h = \frac{5}{2}\cdot\frac{D}{2} = \frac{5}{4}D$, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. The circle has diameter AB = D, so its radius is R = D2.
  2. To just complete the vertical circle, the speed at the top B must satisfy vB2 = gR (normal force zero there).
  3. Energy conservation from A to B: vA2 = vB2 + 2g(2R) = gR + 4gR = 5gR.
  4. Energy conservation on the frictionless track from rest at height h to A: mgh = 12m vA2 = 52mgR, so h = 52R.
  5. h = 52·D2 = 54D, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: Just completing a vertical circle needs v_A^2 = 5gR at the bottom; energy conservation gives gh = 5gR/2, so h = 5R/2 = 5D/4.

question.full_text:
Three objects, A : (a solid sphere), B: (A thin circular disk) and C : (a circular ring), each have the same mass $M$ and radius $R$. They all spin with the same angular speed about their own symmetry axes, The amounts of work ($W$) required to being them to rest, would satisfy the relation
(1) $W_A > W_C > W_B$
(2) $W_C > W_B > W_A$
(3) $W_B > W_A > W_C$
(4) $W_A > W_B > W_C$

  1. (1)WA > WC > WB

They all spin with the same angular speed about their own symmetry axes, The amounts of work ($W$) required to being them to rest, would satisfy the relation

solution.full_text:
1. Accd to work energy theorem, $W = k_f - k_i$
2. Since $k_f = 0$
3. $w \times k_i$
4. $K_A = \frac{1}{2} \times Iw^{2} = \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{2}{5} MR^{2}W^{2}$
5. $K_B = \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} MR^{2}w^{2}$
6. $K_C = \frac{1}{2} MR^{2}w^{2}$
7. So, $W_C > W_B > W_A$
solution.html:
1. Accd to work energy theorem, W = kf - ki
  2. Since kf = 0
  3. w × ki
  4. KA = 12 × Iw2 = 12 × 25 MR2W2
  5. KB = 12 × 12 MR2w2
  6. KC = 12 MR2w2
  7. So, WC > WB > WA
steps: Accd to work energy theorem, $W = k_f - k_i$
Since $k_f = 0$
$w \times k_i$
$K_A = \frac{1}{2} \times Iw^{2} = \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{2}{5} MR^{2}W^{2}$
$K_B = \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} MR^{2}w^{2}$
So, $W_C > W_B > W_A$
By the work-energy theorem, the work needed to stop each body equals its rotational kinetic energy, $W = \frac{1}{2} I \omega^2$.
Since $M$, $R$ and $\omega$ are the same for all three, $W \propto I$.
Solid sphere about a diameter: $I_A = \frac{2}{5} M R^2 = 0.4\, M R^2$.
Thin disk about its symmetry axis: $I_B = \frac{1}{2} M R^2 = 0.5\, M R^2$.
Ring about its symmetry axis: $I_C = M R^2$.
$I_C > I_B > I_A \Rightarrow W_C > W_B > W_A$, which is option $2$.
ai_solution.html:
1. By the work-energy theorem, the work needed to stop each body equals its rotational kinetic energy, W = 12 I ω2.
  2. Since M, R and ω are the same for all three, W ∝ I.
  3. Solid sphere about a diameter: IA = 25 M R2 = 0.4  M R2.
  4. Thin disk about its symmetry axis: IB = 12 M R2 = 0.5  M R2.
  5. Ring about its symmetry axis: IC = M R2.
  6. IC > IB > IA ⇒ WC > WB > WA, which is option 2.
ai_solution.why: Work to stop = rotational KE = (1/2)I w^2; with same M, R, w, I_ring (MR^2) > I_disk (MR^2/2) > I_sphere (2MR^2/5), so W_C > W_B > W_A.

question.full_text:
Which one of the following statements is incorrect?
(1) coefficient of sliding friction has dimensions of length
(2) Rolling friction is smaller than sliding
(3) Friction force opposes the relative motion
(4) Limiting value of static friction is directly proportional to normal reaction
question.html:
Which one of the following statements is incorrect?
  1. (1)coefficient of sliding friction has dimensions of length
  2. (2)Rolling friction is smaller than sliding
  3. (3)Friction force opposes the relative motion
  4. (4)Limiting value of static friction is directly proportional to normal reaction
question.stem: Which one of the following statements is incorrect?

options.text: coefficient of sliding friction has dimensions of length
Rolling friction is smaller than sliding
Friction force opposes the relative motion
Limiting value of static friction is directly proportional to normal reaction

answer.publisher_text: coefficient of sliding friction has dimensions of length
answer.ai_text: coefficient of sliding friction has dimensions of length

solution.full_text: 1. $\mu$ is dimensionless
solution.html: 1. μ is dimensionless
steps: $\mu$ is dimensionless
The coefficient of sliding friction is defined as $\mu_k = \frac{f_k}{N}$.
Both $f_k$ and $N$ are forces with dimensions $[MLT^{-2}]$, so $[\mu_k] = \frac{[MLT^{-2}]}{[MLT^{-2}]} = [M^0L^0T^0]$, i.e. dimensionless, not length; statement $1$ is incorrect.
Rolling friction is smaller than sliding friction, friction opposes relative motion, and $f_s^{max} = \mu_s N$ is directly proportional to $N$, so statements $2$, $3$ and $4$ are correct.
The incorrect statement is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. The coefficient of sliding friction is defined as μk = fkN.
  2. Both fk and N are forces with dimensions [MLT-2], so [μk] = [MLT-2][MLT-2] = [M0L0T0], i.e. dimensionless, not length; statement 1 is incorrect.
  3. Rolling friction is smaller than sliding friction, friction opposes relative motion, and fsmax = μs N is directly proportional to N, so statements 2, 3 and 4 are correct.
  4. The incorrect statement is option 1.
ai_solution.why: Coefficient of friction is a ratio of two forces (f/N), so it is dimensionless and has no dimensions of length; the other three statements are correct.

(2) $0.5$
(3) $0.8$
(4) $0.25$

question.stem: A moving block having mass $m$, collides with another stationary block having mass $4m$ the lighter block comes to rest after collision, When the initial velocity of the lighter block is $v$, then the value of coefficient of restitution$(e)$ will be

solution.full_text:
1. By conservation of linear momentum,
2. $mv + 4m \times 0 = m \times 0 + 4m \times v'$
3. $\Rightarrow v^{1} = \frac{v}{4}$
4. So, $e = \left|\frac{\frac{v}{4} - 0}{vr - 0}\right| = \frac{1}{4} = 0.25$
solution.html:
1. By conservation of linear momentum,
  2. mv + 4m × 0 = m × 0 + 4m × v'
  3. ⇒ v1 = v4
  4. So, e = |v4 - 0vr - 0| = 14 = 0.25
steps: By conservation of linear momentum,
$mv + 4m \times 0 = m \times 0 + 4m \times v'$
$\Rightarrow v^{1} = \frac{v}{4}$
So, $e = \left|\frac{\frac{v}{4} - 0}{vr - 0}\right| = \frac{1}{4} = 0.25$
Linear momentum is conserved: $m v + 4m(0) = m(0) + 4m\,v_2$.
So $v_2 = \frac{v}{4}$.
$e = \frac{1}{4} = 0.25$, which is option $4$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Linear momentum is conserved: m v + 4m(0) = m(0) + 4m v2.
  2. So v2 = v4.
  3. e = v2 - v1u1 - u2 = v4 - 0v - 0.
  4. e = 14 = 0.25, which is option 4.
ai_solution.why: Momentum conservation gives the heavier block v/4; e = separation speed / approach speed = (v/4)/v = 0.25.

trap.label: formula_misused
trap.route: A student carries over the bouncing-ball form $e=\sqrt{h'/h}$, i.e. $e$ as the square root of the kinetic-energy ratio, and gets $\sqrt{\tfrac14}=0.5$; here $e$ is a ratio of relative velocities, which gives $0.25$
trap.who: a student who learnt $e$ through the dropped-ball experiment, where it comes out as a square root of a height or energy ratio
trap.feels: the energy ratio is genuinely $\tfrac14$ in this collision, so its square root looks like the same quantity arrived at a second way

steps.text: Momentum gives the heavy block $v_2 = v/4$, so $KE_f/KE_i = \frac{\frac12(4m)(v/4)^2}{\frac12 m v^2} = \frac14$.
Then $e=\sqrt{KE_f/KE_i}=\sqrt{1/4}=0.5$.
steps.fix: $e$ is defined on velocities, not energies: $e = (v_2-v_1)/(u_1-u_2) = (v/4-0)/v = 0.25$. The square-root form only holds for a ball rebounding off a fixed floor.

other_options.who: a student who remembers that the answer here is a bare mass fraction but not which masses go above and below the line
other_options.feels: $4m/5m=0.8$ is built only from the masses the stem prints, so it looks like the ratio the condition "the lighter block comes to rest" produces

steps.text: The condition that the incoming block stops makes $e$ a pure mass ratio, with no $v$ in it.
Takes that ratio as the struck mass over the total, $4m/(m+4m)=0.8$.
steps.fix: Setting $v_1' = \frac{(m_1-em_2)}{m_1+m_2}u = 0$ gives $e = m_1/m_2 = m/4m = 0.25$.

other_options.proof: Worked every ratio the stem's two masses can form inside a restitution expression: $m_1/m_2 = 0.25$, $m_1/(m_1+m_2) = 0.2$, $m_2/(m_1+m_2) = 0.8$, $(u_1-v_2)/u_1 = 0.75$, and $\sqrt{KE_f/KE_i} = 0.5$. None is $0.4$, and $2/5$ cannot be assembled from $m$ and $4m$ in any of those forms, so it only spreads the options below the answer.

solution.full_text:
1. According to question
2. $I = \frac{E}{nR + R} = \frac{E}{R\left(n + 1\right)}$
3. $\&\ 10I = \frac{E}{\frac{R}{n} + R} = \frac{E}{R\left[1 + \frac{1}{n}\right]}$
4. $\Rightarrow 10 = \frac{\frac{1}{\left(1 + \frac{1}{n}\right)}}{1\left(n + 1\right)} = \frac{n + 1}{1 + \frac{1}{n}} = n$

solution.html:
1. According to question
  2. I = EnR + R = ER(n + 1)
  3. & 10I = ERn + R = ER[1 + 1n]
  4. ⇒ 10 = 1(1 + 1n)1(n + 1) = n + 11 + 1n = n

steps: According to question
$I = \frac{E}{nR + R} = \frac{E}{R\left(n + 1\right)}$
$\&\ 10I = \frac{E}{\frac{R}{n} + R} = \frac{E}{R\left[1 + \frac{1}{n}\right]}$
$\Rightarrow 10 = \frac{\frac{1}{\left(1 + \frac{1}{n}\right)}}{1\left(n + 1\right)} = \frac{n + 1}{1 + \frac{1}{n}} = n$
In series the $n$ resistors give $R_s = nR$, so $I = \frac{E}{nR + R} = \frac{E}{(n+1)R}$.
In parallel the $n$ resistors give $R_p = \frac{R}{n}$.
Then $I' = \frac{E}{\frac{R}{n} + R} = \frac{nE}{(n+1)R} = nI$.
Setting $I' = 10I$ gives $nI = 10I$, so $n = 10$, which is option $2$.

question.stem: A toy car with charge $q$ moves on a frictionless horizontal plane surface under the influence of a uniform electric field $\vec{E}$. Due to the force $q$ ,$\vec{E}$ its velocity increases from 0 to $6\,\mathrm{m/s}$ in one second duration. At that instant the direction of the filed is reversed. The care continues to move for two more seconds under the influence of this field, The average velocity and the average speed of the toy car between 0 to 3 seconds are respectively

solution.full_text:
1. Acceleration, $a = \frac{qE}{m}$
2. $v = u + at$
3. $\Rightarrow 6 = 0 + \frac{qE}{m} \times 1$
4. $\Rightarrow \frac{qE}{m} = 6 = q$ ..........$(1)$
5. From $t = 1$ to $t = 3$, the body retards,
6. $V_f = 6 = \frac{qE}{m} \times 2 = -6\,\mathrm{m/s}$
[Figure: Toy car stages: u = 0 to v = 6 m/s to v = 0 over t = 0, 1, 2, with displacements s1, s2 and the return s3 by t = 3]
7. $CV = 6\,\mathrm{m/s}$
8. $S_1 = \frac{1}{2} \times a \times 1^2 = \frac{1}{2}a \quad \left[s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2\right]$
9. $S_2 = \frac{O^2 - 6^2}{2(-a)} = \frac{18}{a} \quad \left[S = \frac{v^2 - u^2}{29}\right]$
10. $S_3 = \frac{1}{2} \times 9 \times 1^2 = \frac{1}{2}a \quad \left[S = Ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2\right]$
11. Avg Speed $= \frac{\frac{1}{2}a + \frac{18}{a} + \frac{1}{2}a}{3}$
12. Putting $a = 6$
13. $\Rightarrow$ Avg speed $= 3\,\mathrm{m/s}$
14. Avg velocity $= \frac{\frac{1}{2}a + \frac{18}{a} + \frac{1}{2}a}{3}$
15. $= 1\,\mathrm{m/s}$

chapter.name: Kinematics
chapter.why: The answer turns on computing average velocity (net displacement/time) and average speed (total distance/time) for uniformly accelerated motion with a reversal of direction, which is kinematics; the electric field only supplies a constant acceleration.

subtopics.name: Average Velocity
subtopics.why: The answer pairs average velocity (net displacement / total time) with average speed (total distance / total time) over 0-3 s, so it depends on both quantities and on how they differ when motion reverses.

step_list: Find the acceleration from the velocity change 0 to 6 m/s in 1 s (a = 6 m/s^2), and note that reversing the field keeps the same magnitude but flips the sign
Find the displacement in 0-1 s from s = (1/2)at^2 (3 m forward)
After the reversal, find when the car stops (v = 6 - 6t' = 0 at t = 2 s) and the forward distance covered in 1-2 s (3 m)
Find the distance covered moving backward in 2-3 s from rest under the same deceleration (3 m backward)
Combine the parts: net displacement (3 + 3 - 3 m) over 3 s gives the average velocity, total path length (3 + 3 + 3 m) over 3 s gives the average speed
difficulty.why: The motion has to be split into three kinematic segments: uniform acceleration, then deceleration to rest, then acceleration in the reverse direction. Displacement and path length are added separately and each is divided by the 3 s total.
difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: The stem never says that the car turns around at t = 2 s. A candidate who applies s = ut + (1/2)at^2 over the whole 1-3 s interval gets the net displacement right but never sees the 6 m of back-and-forth path, so the average speed comes out equal to the average velocity.

steps: When wedge accelerate s, block, experiences psendo force in opp direction,

printed_lines: When wedge accelerate s, block, experiences psendo force in opp direction,

steps: From the figure, face $AB$ rises to the left at angle $\theta$, so its outward normal points up and to the right, and the wedge accelerates to the right with $a$.
In the wedge frame the block feels gravity $mg$ downward, a pseudo force $ma$ to the left, and the normal force $N$ (smooth surface, no friction).
Resolve along the incline: gravity's down-slope component is $mg\sin\theta$ and the pseudo force's up-slope component is $ma\cos\theta$.
For the block to stay at rest: $ma\cos\theta = mg\sin\theta$.
$a = g\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = g\tan\theta$.
Check in the ground frame: $N\sin\theta = ma$ and $N\cos\theta = mg$ give $\tan\theta = \frac{a}{g}$, the same result, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. From the figure, face AB rises to the left at angle θ, so its outward normal points up and to the right, and the wedge accelerates to the right with a.
  2. In the wedge frame the block feels gravity mg downward, a pseudo force ma to the left, and the normal force N (smooth surface, no friction).
  3. Resolve along the incline: gravity's down-slope component is mgsinθ and the pseudo force's up-slope component is macosθ.
  4. For the block to stay at rest: macosθ = mgsinθ.
  5. a = gsinθcosθ = gtanθ.
  6. Check in the ground frame: Nsinθ = ma and Ncosθ = mg give tanθ = ag, the same result, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: In the wedge frame the pseudo force ma (leftward) has an up-slope component ma cos(theta) that must balance the down-slope gravity component mg sin(theta), so a = g tan(theta).

steps: Divergent evolution produces $\text{homologous}$ organs: the same basic structure from a common ancestor, adapted to different needs.
Forelimbs, brain and heart of bat, man and cheetah (all mammals) share a common vertebrate origin, so options $2$, $3$ and $4$ are homologous, i.e. valid divergent-evolution examples.
The octopus eye (mollusc) and the mammalian eye (bat, man) have different origins but similar function, so they are $\text{analogous}$ organs from convergent evolution.
Hence the incorrect set for divergent evolution is option $1$.

  3. The octopus eye (mollusc) and the mammalian eye (bat, man) have different origins but similar function, so they are analogous organs from convergent evolution.
  4. Hence the incorrect set for divergent evolution is option 1.
ai_solution.why: Divergent evolution gives homologous organs; the eyes of octopus (mollusc) and mammals (bat, man) are analogous organs from convergent evolution, so set 1 is the incorrect example.

steps: The ABO blood group is controlled by one gene $I$ with three alleles $I^A$, $I^B$ and $i$, so it shows multiple alleles (c).
In $I^A I^B$ both antigens are expressed (blood group AB), so $I^A$ and $I^B$ are co-dominant (b).

  2. In IA IB both antigens are expressed (blood group AB), so IA and IB are co-dominant (b).
  3. In IA i and IB i only A or B is expressed, so IA and IB are dominant over i (a).
  4. A single gene is involved and no intermediate phenotype arises, so (d) incomplete dominance and (e) polygenic inheritance do not apply.
  5. The characteristics are a, b and c, which is option 4.
ai_solution.why: ABO blood groups are controlled by three alleles (multiple alleles); I^A and I^B are co-dominant and both are dominant over i (dominance); it is a single gene, so not polygenic, and there is no incomplete dominance.

(1) Pleurodont, Diphyodont, Heterodont
(2) Thecodont, Diphyodont, homodont

(4) Thecodont, Diphyodont, Heterodont

question.stem: Which of the following terms describes human dentition?

solution.full_text: 1. Humans teeth are diphyodont, heterodont and thecodont.
solution.html: 1. Humans teeth are diphyodont, heterodont and thecodont.
steps: Humans teeth are diphyodont, heterodont and thecodont.

steps: Each human tooth is set in a socket of the jaw bone, so the dentition is $\text{thecodont}$, not pleurodont. This rules out options $1$ and $3$.
Humans grow two sets of teeth in a lifetime, milk (deciduous) and permanent, so the dentition is $\text{diphyodont}$.
Humans have four types of teeth: incisors, canines, premolars and molars. So the dentition is $\text{heterodont}$, not homodont, which rules out option $2$.

  2. Humans grow two sets of teeth in a lifetime, milk (deciduous) and permanent, so the dentition is diphyodont.
  3. Humans have four types of teeth: incisors, canines, premolars and molars. So the dentition is heterodont, not homodont, which rules out option 2.
  4. Thecodont + Diphyodont + Heterodont is option 4.
ai_solution.why: Human teeth sit in jaw sockets (thecodont), come in two sets, milk and permanent (diphyodont), and are of four different types (heterodont).

steps.fix: Reabsorption in the PCT is near-isotonic, so it shrinks the volume without concentrating it; the hairpin counter-current of Henle's loop is what builds the concentration gradient.

solution.full_text: 1. The pyramid is inverted pyramid of biomass.
solution.html: 1. The pyramid is inverted pyramid of biomass.
steps: The pyramid is inverted pyramid of biomass.
printed_lines: The pyramid is inverted pyramid of biomass.

steps: The quantities are given in $\mathrm{g}$, so they are standing biomass, giving a pyramid of biomass (not numbers or energy).
Biomass increases upward: $10\,\mathrm{g}$ (producer) $< 60\,\mathrm{g}$ (primary consumer) $< 120\,\mathrm{g}$ (secondary consumer), so the base is smallest and the top is largest.
A pyramid with the smallest base is inverted, so it is an inverted pyramid of biomass, which is option $2$.
ai_solution.html:

  2. Biomass increases upward: 10 g (producer) < 60 g (primary consumer) < 120 g (secondary consumer), so the base is smallest and the top is largest.
  3. A pyramid with the smallest base is inverted, so it is an inverted pyramid of biomass, which is option 2.
ai_solution.why: The data are masses (biomass) that increase from producer (10 g) to secondary consumer (120 g), so the pyramid is an inverted pyramid of biomass.

steps: In glycolysis and the Krebs cycle, dehydrogenases transfer electrons and hydrogen to $\mathrm{NAD^{+}}$, reducing it: $\mathrm{NAD^{+}} + 2e^{-} + 2\mathrm{H^{+}} \rightarrow \mathrm{NADH} + \mathrm{H^{+}}$.
$\mathrm{NADH}$ is reoxidised to $\mathrm{NAD^{+}}$ by passing the electrons to the electron transport system, so $\mathrm{NAD^{+}}$ is an electron carrier, which is option $4$.

ai_solution.html:
1. In glycolysis and the Krebs cycle, dehydrogenases transfer electrons and hydrogen to NAD+, reducing it: NAD+ + 2e- + 2H+ → NADH + H+.

  3. NAD+ is a coenzyme, not an enzyme (rules out option 2), it is not the final electron acceptor (rules out option 1), and it does not supply nucleotides for ATP synthesis (rules out option 3).
ai_solution.why: NAD+ is a coenzyme that accepts electrons/hydrogen (as NADH + H+) in glycolysis and the Krebs cycle and passes them to the electron transport system, so it acts as an electron carrier.

steps: T. H. Morgan worked out linkage in $Drosophila$, so option $1$ is correctly matched.

Starch synthesis in pea is controlled by one gene with two alleles $B$ and $b$; $BB$ gives large grains, $bb$ small, and $Bb$ intermediate, so NCERT uses it for incomplete dominance (dominance being trait-dependent), not multiple alleles. Option $2$ is wrongly matched.

The only wrongly matched pair is option $2$.

  4. In ABO grouping IA and IB are both expressed in IAIB (blood group AB), which is co-dominance, so option 4 is correctly matched.
  5. The only wrongly matched pair is option 2.

steps: $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2Cl} + \mathrm{AlCl_3} \rightarrow \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2^{+}} + \mathrm{AlCl_4^{-}}$.
The primary carbocation undergoes a 1,2-hydride shift to the more stable secondary carbocation: $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2^{+}} \rightarrow \mathrm{(CH_3)_2CH^{+}}$.
Electrophilic substitution on benzene gives $P = \mathrm{C_6H_5CH(CH_3)_2}$ (cumene).
Air oxidation: $\mathrm{C_6H_5CH(CH_3)_2} + \mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_5C(CH_3)_2OOH}$ (cumene hydroperoxide).
Acid hydrolysis with rearrangement: $\mathrm{C_6H_5C(CH_3)_2OOH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_3O^+}/\Delta} \mathrm{C_6H_5OH} + \mathrm{CH_3COCH_3}$, so $Q$ = phenol and $R$ = acetone.
Cumene, phenol and $\mathrm{CH_3-CO-CH_3}$ is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. CH3CH2CH2Cl + AlCl3 → CH3CH2CH2+ + AlCl4-.
  2. The primary carbocation undergoes a 1,2-hydride shift to the more stable secondary carbocation: CH3CH2CH2+ → (CH3)2CH+.
  3. Electrophilic substitution on benzene gives P = C6H5CH(CH3)2 (cumene).
  4. Air oxidation: C6H5CH(CH3)2 + O2 → C6H5C(CH3)2OOH (cumene hydroperoxide).
  5. Acid hydrolysis with rearrangement: C6H5C(CH3)2OOH H3O+/Δ  C6H5OH + CH3COCH3, so Q = phenol and R = acetone.
  6. Cumene, phenol and CH3-CO-CH3 is option 1.
ai_solution.why: Friedel-Crafts alkylation with 1-chloropropane gives cumene via 1 to 2 degree carbocation rearrangement; cumene with O2 then H3O+/heat (cumene process) gives phenol and acetone.

steps: A zwitterion needs an acidic group and a basic group in the same molecule, so that a proton moves from one to the other.
Glycine, $\mathrm{H_2N{-}CH_2{-}COOH}$, has both: $\mathrm{H_2N{-}CH_2{-}COOH \rightarrow H_3\overset{+}{N}{-}CH_2{-}COO^-}$.

Aniline ($\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2}$) has only a basic group, benzoic acid ($\mathrm{C_6H_5COOH}$) only an acidic group, and acetanilide ($\mathrm{C_6H_5NHCOCH_3}$) has a non-basic amide N and no acidic group.
So only glycine forms a zwitterion, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. A zwitterion needs an acidic group and a basic group in the same molecule, so that a proton moves from one to the other.
  2. Glycine, H2N-CH2-COOH, has both: H2N-CH2-COOH → H3+N-CH2-COO-.
  3. Aniline (C6H5NH2) has only a basic group, benzoic acid (C6H5COOH) only an acidic group, and acetanilide (C6H5NHCOCH3) has a non-basic amide N and no acidic group.
  4. So only glycine forms a zwitterion, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: Glycine is an amino acid with both a basic -NH2 and an acidic -COOH group, so an internal proton transfer gives the dipolar ion H3N+-CH2-COO-; the other compounds lack one of the two groups (or the amine is non-basic amide).

question.stem: The geometry and magnetic behaviour of the complex $[\mathrm{Ni(Co)_4}]$ are

solution.full_text:
1. $[\mathrm{Ni(CO)4}]$ is diamagnetic and assumes tetrahedral structure.
2. Carbonyl is a strong ligand and involves force pairing.
3. Hence correct option is $4$
solution.html:
1. [Ni(CO)4] is diamagnetic and assumes tetrahedral structure.
  2. Carbonyl is a strong ligand and involves force pairing.
  3. Hence correct option is 4
steps: $[\mathrm{Ni(CO)4}]$ is diamagnetic and assumes tetrahedral structure.
Carbonyl is a strong ligand and involves force pairing.
Hence correct option is $4$
printed_lines: is diamagnetic and assumes tetrahedral structure.
Carbonyl is a strong ligand and involves force pairing. Hence correct option is 4

steps: In $[\mathrm{Ni(CO)_4}]$ each CO is neutral, so the oxidation state of Ni is $0$.
Ground state $\mathrm{Ni}(0)$: $[\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^{8}\,4s^{2}$.
CO is a strong-field ligand, so the $4s$ electrons are pushed into $3d$, giving $3d^{10}\,4s^{0}$.
The four CO ligands donate into the empty $4s$ and three $4p$ orbitals: $sp^{3}$ hybridisation, so the geometry is tetrahedral.
With $3d^{10}$ all electrons are paired, so the number of unpaired electrons is $0$ and the complex is diamagnetic.
Tetrahedral and diamagnetic is option $4$.
ai_solution.html:
1. In [Ni(CO)4] each CO is neutral, so the oxidation state of Ni is 0.
  2. Ground state Ni(0): [Ar] 3d8 4s2.
  3. CO is a strong-field ligand, so the 4s electrons are pushed into 3d, giving 3d10 4s0.
  4. The four CO ligands donate into the empty 4s and three 4p orbitals: sp3 hybridisation, so the geometry is tetrahedral.
  5. With 3d10 all electrons are paired, so the number of unpaired electrons is 0 and the complex is diamagnetic.
  6. Tetrahedral and diamagnetic is option 4.
ai_solution.why: In Ni(CO)4, Ni is in the 0 state; strong-field CO pairs the 3d electrons (3d10), giving sp3 hybridisation: tetrahedral with no unpaired electrons, so diamagnetic.

solution.full_text:
1. $\mathrm{Co^{3+}}$ contains $4$ unpaired electrons, $\mu = \sqrt{24}\,\mathrm{B.M.}$
2. $\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}$ contains $3$ unpaired electrons, $\mu = \sqrt{15}\,\mathrm{B.M.}$
3. $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}$ contains $5$ unpaired electrons, $\mu = \sqrt{35}\,\mathrm{B.M.}$
4. $\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}$ contains $2$ unpaired electrons, $\mu = \sqrt{8}\,\mathrm{B.M.}$
5. Therefore the correct option is 2

  2. Cr3+ contains 3 unpaired electrons, μ = 15 B.M.

$\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}$ contains $3$ unpaired electrons, $\mu = \sqrt{15}\,\mathrm{B.M.}$

$\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}$ contains $2$ unpaired electrons, $\mu = \sqrt{8}\,\mathrm{B.M.}$
Therefore the correct option is 2
Spin-only magnetic moment: $\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}\,\mathrm{B.M}$, where $n$ is the number of unpaired electrons (free ions).
$\mathrm{Co^{3+}}$: $[\mathrm{Ar}]3d^6$, $n = 4$, $\mu = \sqrt{4 \times 6} = \sqrt{24}\,\mathrm{B.M}$, so a-iv.
$\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}$: $[\mathrm{Ar}]3d^3$, $n = 3$, $\mu = \sqrt{3 \times 5} = \sqrt{15}\,\mathrm{B.M}$, so b-v.
$\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}$: $[\mathrm{Ar}]3d^5$, $n = 5$, $\mu = \sqrt{5 \times 7} = \sqrt{35}\,\mathrm{B.M}$, so c-ii.
$\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}$: $[\mathrm{Ar}]3d^8$, $n = 2$, $\mu = \sqrt{2 \times 4} = \sqrt{8}\,\mathrm{B.M}$, so d-i.
The match a-iv, b-v, c-ii, d-i is option $2$.

  3. Cr3+: [Ar]3d3, n = 3, μ = 3 × 5 = 15 B.M, so b-v.
  4. Fe3+: [Ar]3d5, n = 5, μ = 5 × 7 = 35 B.M, so c-ii.
  5. Ni2+: [Ar]3d8, n = 2, μ = 2 × 4 = 8 B.M, so d-i.
  6. The match a-iv, b-v, c-ii, d-i is option 2.

question.full_text:
The type of isomerism shown by the complex $\mathrm{[CoCl_2(en)_2]}$ is.
(1) Linkage isomerism
(2) Geometrical isomerism
(3) Ionization isomerism
(4) Coordination isomerism
question.html:
The type of isomerism shown by the complex [CoCl2(en)2] is.
  1. (1)Linkage isomerism
  2. (2)Geometrical isomerism
  3. (3)Ionization isomerism
  4. (4)Coordination isomerism
question.stem: The type of isomerism shown by the complex $\mathrm{[CoCl_2(en)_2]}$ is.

solution.full_text:
1. $[\mathrm{CoCl_2(en)_2}]$ shows geometrical isomerism
2. Hence the correct option is 2
solution.html:
1. [CoCl2(en)2] shows geometrical isomerism
  2. Hence the correct option is 2
steps: $[\mathrm{CoCl_2(en)_2}]$ shows geometrical isomerism
Hence the correct option is 2
$\mathrm{[CoCl_2(en)_2]}$ is an octahedral complex of type $\mathrm{M(AA)_2B_2}$, with $\mathrm{en}$ bidentate and two monodentate $\mathrm{Cl^-}$.
The two $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ ligands can sit adjacent (cis) or opposite (trans), so the complex shows geometrical isomerism.
$\mathrm{Cl^-}$ and $\mathrm{en}$ are not ambidentate, so linkage isomerism is ruled out.
There is no counter-ion to exchange with a ligand and no second complex ion, so ionization and coordination isomerism are ruled out; the answer is option $2$.
ai_solution.html:
1. [CoCl2(en)2] is an octahedral complex of type M(AA)2B2, with en bidentate and two monodentate Cl-.
  2. The two Cl- ligands can sit adjacent (cis) or opposite (trans), so the complex shows geometrical isomerism.
  3. Cl- and en are not ambidentate, so linkage isomerism is ruled out.
  4. There is no counter-ion to exchange with a ligand and no second complex ion, so ionization and coordination isomerism are ruled out; the answer is option 2.
ai_solution.why: [CoCl2(en)2] is an octahedral MA2(AA)2 complex, so the two Cl ligands can be cis or trans: geometrical isomerism (the cis form is also optically active).

  3. (3)MnO4-
  4. (4)Cr2O72-
question.stem: Which one of the following ions exhibits d-d transition and paramagnetism as well?

solution.full_text:
1. $\mathrm{MnO_4^{2-}}$ , the oxidation state of $\mathrm{Mn}$ is $+6$.
2. It will have one unpaired electron.
3. Hence it will exhibit paramagnetic behavior and also involves $d$-$d$ transition.
4. Hence the correct option is 1
solution.html:
1. MnO42- , the oxidation state of Mn is +6.
  2. It will have one unpaired electron.
  3. Hence it will exhibit paramagnetic behavior and also involves d-d transition.
  4. Hence the correct option is 1
steps: $\mathrm{MnO_4^{2-}}$ , the oxidation state of $\mathrm{Mn}$ is $+6$.
It will have one unpaired electron.
Hence it will exhibit paramagnetic behavior and also involves $d$-$d$ transition.
Hence the correct option is 1
printed_lines: MnO_{4}^{2-} , the oxidation state of Mn is +6. It will have one unpaired electron. Hence it will
exhibit paramagnetic behavior and also involves d-d transition.

steps: A d-d transition and paramagnetism both need at least one unpaired $d$ electron, so the metal ion must not be $d^0$.
$\mathrm{MnO_4^{2-}}$: $x - 8 = -2 \Rightarrow x = +6$; $\mathrm{Mn^{6+}}$ is $[\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^1$, one unpaired electron.
$\mathrm{CrO_4^{2-}}$: $x - 8 = -2 \Rightarrow x = +6$; $\mathrm{Cr^{6+}}$ is $3d^0$, diamagnetic.
$\mathrm{MnO_4^{-}}$: $x - 8 = -1 \Rightarrow x = +7$; $\mathrm{Mn^{7+}}$ is $3d^0$, diamagnetic.
$\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}}$: $2x - 14 = -2 \Rightarrow x = +6$; $\mathrm{Cr^{6+}}$ is $3d^0$, diamagnetic.
Only $\mathrm{MnO_4^{2-}}$ ($3d^1$) is both paramagnetic and capable of a d-d transition, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. A d-d transition and paramagnetism both need at least one unpaired d electron, so the metal ion must not be d0.
  2. MnO42-: x - 8 = -2 ⇒ x = +6; Mn6+ is [Ar] 3d1, one unpaired electron.
  3. CrO42-: x - 8 = -2 ⇒ x = +6; Cr6+ is 3d0, diamagnetic.
  4. MnO4-: x - 8 = -1 ⇒ x = +7; Mn7+ is 3d0, diamagnetic.
  5. Cr2O72-: 2x - 14 = -2 ⇒ x = +6; Cr6+ is 3d0, diamagnetic.
  6. Only MnO42- (3d1) is both paramagnetic and capable of a d-d transition, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: In MnO4^2- Mn is +6 (3d1): one unpaired electron gives paramagnetism and allows a d-d transition; Cr(+6) in CrO4^2- and Cr2O7^2- and Mn(+7) in MnO4^- are d0, so they are diamagnetic with no d-d transition.

steps: Each structure is an arenium ($\sigma$-complex) ion formed when $Y^+$ attacks nitrobenzene; label the carbon bearing $-NO_2$ as $C_1$.
In a cyclohexadienyl cation the $+$ charge is spread over the 1st, 3rd and 5th carbons of the pentadienyl chain, i.e. the carbons ortho and para to the $sp^3$ carbon.
Options $1$ and $4$ place $+$ directly on $C_1$, next to the strongly $-I/-R$ $NO_2$ group: highly destabilised.
Option $2$ has the $sp^3$ carbon para to $C_1$, so its resonance hybrid also has a contributor with $+$ on $C_1$: destabilised.
Option $3$ has the $sp^3$ carbon meta to $C_1$, so $+$ is delocalised only over $C_2, C_4, C_6$ and never sits on $C_1$; the drawn $+$ at $C_4$ is also farthest from $NO_2$ (weakest $-I$).
Hence option $3$ (the meta-attack $\sigma$-complex) is the most stable carbocation.
ai_solution.html:
1. Each structure is an arenium (σ-complex) ion formed when Y+ attacks nitrobenzene; label the carbon bearing -NO2 as C1.
  2. In a cyclohexadienyl cation the + charge is spread over the 1st, 3rd and 5th carbons of the pentadienyl chain, i.e. the carbons ortho and para to the sp3 carbon.
  3. Options 1 and 4 place + directly on C1, next to the strongly -I/-R NO2 group: highly destabilised.
  4. Option 2 has the sp3 carbon para to C1, so its resonance hybrid also has a contributor with + on C1: destabilised.
  5. Option 3 has the sp3 carbon meta to C1, so + is delocalised only over C2, C4, C6 and never sits on C1; the drawn + at C4 is also farthest from NO2 (weakest -I).
  6. Hence option 3 (the meta-attack σ-complex) is the most stable carbocation.
ai_solution.why: All four are sigma complexes of Y attacking nitrobenzene; only option 3 (meta attack) can never place the positive charge on the carbon bearing the strongly electron-withdrawing NO2 group, so it is the most stable.

chapter.why: The answer turns on how the electron-withdrawing NO2 group (inductive/resonance effect) destabilises a positive charge placed on or next to the carbon bearing it, so the cation whose charge stays away from that carbon is most stable, which is carbocation stability taught in General Organic Chemistry.

subtopics.name: Resonance Effect
subtopics.why: The answer depends on where the ring positive charge sits relative to the electron-withdrawing NO2 group, whose -R (-M) effect destabilises a positive charge at the ortho/para (ipso) positions but not at the meta position, which is the case in option 2.

step_list: Recognise the four structures as arenium-ion (sigma-complex) forms from attack of Y+ on nitrobenzene, and recall that -NO2 is strongly electron-withdrawing (-I, -M), so it destabilises a positive charge, most of all when the charge is on the carbon carrying NO2
Read each ring to place the positive charge relative to the NO2-bearing carbon and the sp3 C(H)(Y) carbon
Eliminate options 1 and 4, where the positive charge sits directly on the carbon bearing NO2
Choose between options 2 and 3, where the charge is off the NO2 carbon in both, by how far the charge is from NO2, using the fact that the inductive pull weakens with distance
difficulty.why: The work is reading four ring drawings to find where the positive charge sits relative to the NO2 group, using the electron-withdrawing effect of NO2 to rule out two options, then separating the last two by how far the charge is from NO2.
difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: Two options (2 and 3) both keep the positive charge off the NO2-bearing carbon, so the usual rule that the charge must not sit next to an EWG leaves two candidates. The final choice depends on a finer argument about how the inductive effect falls off with distance and needs careful reading of the tilted ring drawings. The substituent Y is never specified, so the candidate must assume it is the same in every option.

steps: The $-I$ effect of a substituent grows with the electronegativity of the atom bonded to the chain: $\mathrm{F} > \mathrm{O} > \mathrm{N}$.
So $-\mathrm{F} > -\mathrm{OR} > -\mathrm{NR_2}$ and $-\mathrm{F} > -\mathrm{OR} > -\mathrm{NH_2}$ in $-I$ strength; alkyl groups on N only lower the $-I$ of $-\mathrm{NR_2}$ further.
Options $1$ and $3$ give the reverse order, so both are false.

Option $2$ ($-\mathrm{NH_2} < -\mathrm{OR} < -\mathrm{F}$) and option $4$ ($-\mathrm{NR_2} < -\mathrm{OR} < -\mathrm{F}$) both hold; option $4$ is chosen as it compares alkyl-substituted N and O groups, matching the given $\mathrm{R}$ = alkyl.
ai_solution.html:
1. The -I effect of a substituent grows with the electronegativity of the atom bonded to the chain: F > O > N.
  2. So -F > -OR > -NR2 and -F > -OR > -NH2 in -I strength; alkyl groups on N only lower the -I of -NR2 further.
  3. Options 1 and 3 give the reverse order, so both are false.
  4. Option 2 (-NH2 < -OR < -F) and option 4 (-NR2 < -OR < -F) both hold; option 4 is chosen as it compares alkyl-substituted N and O groups, matching the given R = alkyl.
ai_solution.why: -I effect follows electronegativity of the attached atom F > O > N, so -NR2 < -OR < -F; but -NH2 < -OR < -F (option 2) is equally true, so two options look correct.

question.stem: The solubility of $\mathrm{BaSO_4}$in water is $2.42\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{g\,L^{-1}}$ at $298\,\mathrm{K}$, The value of its solubility product ($K_{sp}$) will be (Given molar mass of $\mathrm{BaSO_4}$ = $233\,\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$)

solution.full_text:
1. $\mathrm{BaSO4} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{Ba^{2+}} + \mathrm{SO_{4}^{2-}}$
2. $\mathrm{Ksp} = [\mathrm{Ba^{2+}}]\,[\,\mathrm{So_{4}^{2-}}]$
3. $\mathrm{Ksp} = \mathrm{S^{2}}$
4. Hence the correct option is 2
solution.html:
1. BaSO4 ⇌ Ba2+ + SO42-
  2. Ksp = [Ba2+] [ So42-]
  3. Ksp = S2
  4. Hence the correct option is 2
steps: $\mathrm{BaSO4} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{Ba^{2+}} + \mathrm{SO_{4}^{2-}}$
$\mathrm{Ksp} = [\mathrm{Ba^{2+}}]\,[\,\mathrm{So_{4}^{2-}}]$
$\mathrm{Ksp} = \mathrm{S^{2}}$
Hence the correct option is 2
Convert the mass solubility to molar solubility: $s = \frac{2.42\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{g\,L^{-1}}}{233\,\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}} = 1.0386\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$.
$\mathrm{BaSO_4(s) \rightleftharpoons Ba^{2+}(aq) + SO_4^{2-}(aq)}$, so $[\mathrm{Ba^{2+}}] = [\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}] = s$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Convert the mass solubility to molar solubility: s = 2.42×10-3 g L-1233 g mol-1 = 1.0386×10-5 mol L-1.
  2. BaSO4(s) ⇌ Ba2+(aq) + SO42-(aq), so [Ba2+] = [SO42-] = s.
  3. Ksp = [Ba2+][SO42-] = s2.
  4. Ksp = (1.0386×10-5)2 = 1.0787×10-10 ≈ 1.08×10-10 mol2 L-2, which is option 2.
ai_solution.why: Molar solubility s = 2.42e-3/233 = 1.04e-5 mol/L; for BaSO4 (1:1 salt) Ksp = s^2 = 1.08e-10 mol^2 L^-2.
